doc.title: Josephine Davies interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, October 14, 2025

title: Describing her music to venues; Café Oto, 'Isfahan' and 12-bar blues
summary: She calls Satori contemporary jazz, finds categories hard for booking, and enjoys playing Strayhorn's 'Isfahan' and blues.

story.theme_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and rough clubs of Prohibition
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: What’s the average venue that you try to book, and I’m wondering if you’re required sometimes to explain what it is you’re doing if a club owner asks you -- well it’s not enough these days to say we play jazz. “Well what do you play? Trad jazz? Or do you do fusion?” Do you have an answer at the ready for that kind of situation?

It’s rough. It’s so difficult that one. And I sort of say, depending on the project, but with Satori I say it’s contemporary jazz. We do originals. And I might say sometimes in this – influenced by a certain person or it might seem that – if I’m trying to get a gig somewhere where they don’t necessarily know me I might look on my website and see who’s played that fits my genre I suppose, that is doing something similarly contemporary but not way out, kind of squeaky, honky, free jazz. And that’s not playing trad jazz or you know maybe bebop, something like that, bebop, hard bop, that sense of, it would be good to just make sure that they’re not expecting some Charlie Parker numbers and that we are going to be doing something perhaps more modern. But it is really difficult. And it’s funny, what I’ve noticed is with the trio is because we play, there’s a lot of free improvisation within it but there are still melodies and hooks and harmonic progressions, rhythmic things, all of that sort of stuff, some swing. It doesn’t fit, say like Café Oto is perhaps the most famous venue in London for free jazz and it’s really, you know, really left field. It’s out there and you get to see some stuff that seems like just people are, you know that question is, “Is this music?” You know, that sort of just brought a load of kitchen utensils and they’re throwing toy trains at them. That kind of thing. So I don’t think it would work in there because it might be too jazz. But at the same time there are other venues who say it’s too free or it’s too experimental. So it’s kind of difficult because I don’t want to particularly categorize myself so much that I can’t just do what I want to do. And in fact we did a gig the other day and I can’t remember why, I was really moved to play “Isfahan.” So we did “Isfahan” as a trio at the end of the night. It was great. It was so satisfying just to pop that in. And why not? You know Billy Strayhorn was an incredible composer. And it didn’t feel any different from the rest of the gig you know, it didn’t feel like oh we’ve run out of tunes, let’s play a 12- bar blues.
Do you ever do that? Play a 12-bar blues?
Yeah I love playing a 12-bar blues.

I’m glad you said that. You know compared to other free jazz I’ve heard, and I’m more into Cannonball Adderley and soul jazz personally, but your music felt less demonstrative and more inviting I think than a lot of, I’ll still use the term free jazz. It’s an observation, not really a question. Perhaps, I’ve seen some comments on your playing
